title: Shammai's measuring stick (Shabbat 31a)
hookLine: the same man went first to Shammai, who pushed him away with a builder's rod

lines: FIRST HE KNOCKED ON SHAMMAI'S DOOR.
A BUILDER'S ROD IN HIS HAND.
cards: Here's the part of yesterday's story that usually gets cut. Before the man ever reached Hillel, he knocked on another door: Shammai's, the other great sage of the generation. Same request.
Teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai had a builder's measuring rod in his hand. He pushed the man away with it.
Only then did the man go to Hillel. So why does the Talmud bother to tell us?

teach.b: The Talmud calls it the builder's cubit, a straight rod for measuring. It fits. Shammai measured things exactly, and a question that didn't measure up got pushed out the door.
The same page tells two more stories like it.
One man wants to accept only the written Torah, not the oral teaching. Another wants to convert so he can become high priest.
Each time Shammai sends him away, and each time Hillel takes him in and teaches him patiently, until the man sees for himself.
Right before these, the Talmud tells of a man who bet four hundred coins that he could make Hillel lose his temper.
He knocked on Hillel's door on Friday afternoon, while Hillel was washing for Shabbat, and asked silly questions. Why are Babylonians' heads round? Hillel came out, answered kindly, and went back in.
Again and again. The man lost his bet. So the Talmud draws a lesson: a person should always be humble and patient like Hillel, and not strict and impatient like Shammai.
But Shammai isn't a villain. He was one of the great teachers, and his school's views are kept in the Mishnah beside Hillel's.
His own well-known saying, in Pirkei Avot: receive every person with a cheerful face.
Maybe that was the lesson he taught himself. The measuring stick is real. So is the cheerful face.

how: Jewish teachers often retell the stories of Hillel and Shammai together; the saying about being patient like Hillel is quoted to encourage kindness toward questioners and newcomers.

games.q: it's Friday afternoon. you're washing for Shabbat. a stranger at the door asks why Babylonians' heads are round. again. what do you do?
o: tell him to come back next week.
games.why: Hillel came out, answered gently, and went back in, again and again. the man lost his bet of four hundred coins.

practice: This week ran from not judging the jug by its outside, through four kinds of people, what the Talmud is, page two and the first question, to the whole Torah on one foot.

Now picture a question that tests your patience, a child's fifth why, a coworker asking the same thing again, and feel the rod in your hand. Then put it down, and answer the way Hillel did, kindly, one more time.

wordCard.voice: Shammai, the great sage whose builder's rod pushed away a strange question, giving the Talmud its reason to say: be patient like Hillel.

orig.note: Hebrew: the builder's cubit, the measuring rod Shammai held.

carryVoice: Your line: be patient like Hillel. That's a week of Talmud, and a good one. Day two hundred seventy-three.
